Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-06-23

Attendees: Alex Kim, Priya Shah (Redwood); Jordan Lee, Aisha Martinez, Evan Park (NovaRetail)

---
Auto Summary (may be imperfect):
Alex walked through this week's cache hit numbers and the small config changes. Aisha ran the last seeding job; we saw hit rates jump but still under target. Agreed to try more aggressive prompt normalization, extend TTLs for certain prefix patterns, and run a 24-hour warm-up. Redwood to send configs and seeding script.

---
Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Kim: ok uh hey everyone thanks for joining i think we have about 35 minutes, um quick roll call?
[00:05] Jordan Lee: hey jordan here, aisha and evan are with me
[00:07] Aisha Martinez: hi all
[00:08] Evan Park: yep hi
[00:09] Priya Shah: priya from redwood, se on this POC
[00:12] Alex Kim: cool alright goal for today is to review hit rates, what changed since last week, and agree next steps for warm up and keying. i tossed the benchmark sheet into the chat, link is the redwood benchmark csv, uh if anyone needs it again i can re-share
[00:30] Jordan Lee: saw it, thanks
[00:33] Alex Kim: quick highlight: after Aisha's prompt dedupe run plus canonicalization we moved prefix cache hit from ~12% to 48% on the session workloads that have high prompt reuse, so big jump but not yet at our 60% internal target. p50 latency improved from about 220ms to 160ms for cached requests, p95 still around 620ms for cold paths.
[01:02] Aisha Martinez: yeah that matches what we saw, though a lot of the low hanging fruit was identical prompts across users. once we normalized templates and removed trailing whitespace we got a lot more reuse. some of our bots attach dynamic metadata to the prompt that leaks tokens so that's still hurting us.
[01:25] Evan Park: question: are we keying based on the full prompt text or do you do a prefix hash? we saw a lot of near-duplicates that weren't exact matches
[01:34] Priya Shah: currently default is full prompt hash, alex changed to prefix-keying for the top 128 tokens in the last config, that helped. but we recommend canonicalization + template extraction before hashing. so strip user-specific metadata, stable ids, timestamps, all that.
[01:50] Jordan Lee: can you explain prefix vs kv cache? i'm using kv cache and i'm not sure i'm understanding the separation
[01:56] Alex Kim: yeah good q. so prefix cache here is really the higher-level caching layer that looks at prompt prefixes and maps to cached KV entries, the kv cache itself is the transformer key/value cache for autoregressive decoding — different but related. folks sometimes call both KV but in our stack we have a prefix-layer that returns a cached token stream and also a lower-level KV cache for stateful decoding. sorry if that's confusing in the docs.
[02:24] Aisha Martinez: no it's helpful, thanks.
[02:28] Alex Kim: no worries. this POC we've been playing with both: prefix-level reuse for identical prompt generations, and strategic KV reuse for session continuity.
[02:36] Priya Shah: quick note — we saw the most gains by canonicalizing prompts and then limiting key length to 128 tokens for hashing. that keeps similar prompts from diverging due to long tail metadata. also some models are super sensitive to tokenization differences, so we recommended run tokenizers as part of canonicalization.
[02:58] Jordan Lee: got it. aisha — you ran a short seeding job last night, what's the 12h result?
[03:05] Aisha Martinez: yes 12h run: baseline day (no seeding) avg hit 12%; after the dedupe + canonicalization and 12h seeding we got to 48% avg hit. p50 latency for cached requests is 160ms, cold requests 480-650ms depending on sequence length. cost estimate we crunched is about 18% savings at the current qps for token compute.
[03:36] Evan Park: nice. what about burst safety? we saw a large spike last week and cache warmed but then thundering herd caused some backend load
[03:44] Priya Shah: we recommend staggered warm-up and a small backoff jitter on the seeding job to avoid thundering herd. also set an upper bound on concurrent warm-up requests; Redwood's seeder script has that parameter.
[03:58] Alex Kim: also note TTL tuning matters — for high-reuse prefixes we set TTL to 24 hours, for ephemeral prompts 1 hour. that reduced churn in the hot set.
[04:11] Jordan Lee: hmm 24 hours sounds long, our data retention policy... will that cause PII exposure?
[04:17] Aisha Martinez: we also worry about storing user PHI in cache keys, even if encrypted.
[04:22] Priya Shah: totally valid. we suggest redaction at canonicalization: redwood offers rules to remove PII fields or replace with stable placeholders before hashing. plus if you run private deployment you can keep the cache in your VPC, encrypted at rest with your KMS.
[04:38] Evan Park: can you share the encryption notes again? the SOC2 checklist we saw earlier didn't include cache specifics
[04:44] Alex Kim: yes we'll include KMS/HSM integration notes and the SOC2 annex in the packet we send. action item for us to attach those docs.
[04:54] Jordan Lee: thanks. about keying strategy — for near-duplicates should we fuzzy-hash or use template extraction?
[05:01] Priya Shah: template extraction is higher-signal: detect variable slots and map them to placeholders, then hash the template. fuzzy hashing can help but risks collisions if thresholds aren't tuned. we prefer deterministic template extraction plus optional n-gram fingerprinting as a fallback.
[05:18] Aisha Martinez: we tried fuzzy last month and got some false hits causing wrong canned responses, so we moved away.
[05:25] Alex Kim: yeah that matches other customers — template-based canonicalization tends to be safer for correctness.
[05:31] Evan Park: what's the operational footprint? we have a managed Redis cluster for session state today; do you recommend putting the prefix layer in Redis too or use in-memory on the inference tier?
[05:42] Priya Shah: tradeoffs: in-memory on the inference node gives lowest latency but doesn't scale across nodes unless you have sharding; Redis centralizes the hot set but adds network hops. for NovaRetail scale we saw Redis with local LRU cache at node-level as a sweet spot. also consider replication factor and read replicas for failover.
[06:02] Jordan Lee: okay and costs? network egress to Redis vs local mem?
[06:07] Alex Kim: network egress is small relative to token compute for most configs, but if you have very high qps then the network cost can add up. our Optimize toolkit can estimate that from your qps. we'll include an estimate in the sheet.
[06:20] Aisha Martinez: great. next: we've got some errors in our logs where the cache key generation sometimes uses session id instead of template, causing low reuse. any quick guardrails?
[06:31] Priya Shah: yes add validation rules in the canonicalizer: if template length < threshold or if placeholders > x% then fallback to full-text hashing or mark as non-cacheable. basically allow an explicit "no-cache" tag on prompts from the app if needed.
[06:48] Evan Park: can Redwood set that no-cache flag from the SDK?
[06:51] Alex Kim: yep SDK supports per-request cache control headers — cache-control style TTL and a no-cache boolean.
[06:58] Jordan Lee: ok good.
[07:01] Alex Kim: quick demo of week's numbers — (screen briefly) the sheet shows per-route hit rates, we highlighted the top 10 routes by QPS; those are where most wins are. Aisha, does that align with your telemetry?
[07:18] Aisha Martinez: yes top 3 routes are the chat assistants and the product-recommendation generator. the recommendation route is high variance with long dynamic metadata on each request.
[07:29] Priya Shah: recommendation route is a good candidate for templateization: strip the dynamic context into a secondary input vector instead of inlining into prompt. then you can canonicalize the prompt and pass context via structured fields or tool calls.
[07:45] Jordan Lee: hmm that might need app changes — what's the lift?
[07:48] Alex Kim: small code change in microservice: separate templated prompt and context payload, 1-2 engineers for a sprint maybe. Priya can share a recipe.
[07:59] Aisha Martinez: ok we can evaluate that.
[08:02] Evan Park: about measuring correctness — if we cache a previously generated token stream for a template but the structured context changes, we might return stale content
[08:12] Priya Shah: yep that's why keys must include stable indicators of context that affect output. if the context is passed as a tool call or a different channel we can avoid caching on that axis.
[08:24] Jordan Lee: are there metrics we should monitor besides hit-rate and latency?
[08:28] Alex Kim: yes: cache churn rate, false-hit rate (where cached response was semantically invalid and triggered fallback), cost-per-request, and distribution of TTL expirations. we can push those to your dashboard.
[08:40] Aisha Martinez: will you add false-hit detection in the next chart? that's super helpful
[08:44] Alex Kim: yes we'll add a false-hit column in the benchmark CSV.
[08:47] Evan Park: security check — if we use managed Redis in the hosted flow, is there egress to third-party cloud?
[08:54] Priya Shah: managed Redis from Redwood is in the same region and under Redwood's infra; we can also use your managed Redis in VPC peering in Dedicated/Private modes to keep data in your account. encryption in transit and at rest supported.
[09:07] Jordan Lee: ok i'd prefer VPC peered redis for compliance.
[09:10] Alex Kim: noted — we'll document the network options and a sample Terraform snippet for peering.
[09:18] Priya Shah: quick question to NovaRetail: what's the traffic shape overnight? do you expect hot sets to cool off and then rebuild in morning causing inconsistent UX?
[09:27] Aisha Martinez: we have a big morning ramp from 6-9am, and nights are light. so warm-up before peak is critical.
[09:34] Alex Kim: so recommended pattern: run a rolling warm-up between 5:15-5:45am with jitter and limited concurrency, then keep a small persistent seeder updating high-value keys every hour. that keeps the hot set stable.
[09:50] Evan Park: how invasive is the seeder? does it generate real logs or telemetry we need to filter?
[09:55] Priya Shah: seeder requests look like normal requests and will produce telemetry; we include flags to mark them as synthetic so you can filter them out from business analytics.
[10:06] Jordan Lee: ok thanks. last area: do you have any recommendations for quantization interplay with KV cache? we plan to run int8 models on dedicated nodes
[10:14] Alex Kim: good Q — quantization affects tokenization and sometimes determinism. KV cache keys should be generated pre-quantization (i.e., at prompt canonicalization time) and be model-agnostic where possible. if you're switching model variants you may need model-version in the key.
[10:29] Aisha Martinez: noted, we'll add model-version when doing A/Bing.
[10:33] Alex Kim: cool ok let's recap action items and owners.
[10:36] Priya Shah: alex — send annotated benchmark and SOC2/KMS notes.
[10:40] Alex Kim: yep will do, and priya will drop seeding script and Redis examples. aisha will run 24 hour seeding and post results, evan will validate VPC peering constraints.
[10:50] Jordan Lee: can we get an SOW estimate if we ask Redwood to run the warm-up operationally?
[10:55] Alex Kim: yes we'll include a rough ops estimate in the followup and a recommended SOW for managed warm-up and tuning.
[11:03] Aisha Martinez: timeline wise we aim to hit 60% hit-rate by end of next week, that seems realistic if the 24h seeding holds.
[11:11] Alex Kim: great, we can support that. ok thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the docs and meeting notes.
[11:18] Jordan Lee: thanks all
[11:19] Evan Park: thanks
[11:20] Priya Shah: thanks
